issues.legal_issue: A temporary injunction is not justified where the plaintiff has a prima facie case but the injury alleged can be adequately compensated by damages.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought a temporary injunction to prevent the defendants from leasing, transferring, or encumbering the premises while a suit for specific performance was pending.

The agreement included a term requiring the agent to retain possession of the premises during the agreement, and the court found that the plaintiff had a prima facie case concerning breach of that term.
The plaintiff pleaded an alternative claim for damages and set out monetary estimates for projected lost profits, loss of goodwill, and relocation costs.
The alleged injury was financial, and the court concluded that damages could compensate the plaintiff if it succeeded in the suit.
issues.conclusion: The temporary injunction was not warranted because the plaintiff would not suffer irreparable injury; the injunction orders were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order 39 Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a court considering temporary injunction must assess prima facie case, balance of convenience, and irreparable injury. A prima facie case alone is insufficient: under Dalpat Kumar v. Prahlad Singh, (1992) 1 SCC 719, the injury must be material and not adequately compensable by damages. Kishoresinh Ratansinh Jadeja v. Maruti Corporation, (2009) 11 SCC 229, states the three-part test. Irreparable injury is injury that cannot be compensated by a decree, as explained in The Attorney-General v. Hallett, (1857) 16 M. & W. 569.

rule.if: temporary_injunction_application and prima_facie_case and alternative_damages_claimed and financial_injury_compensable_by_damages

predicates.temporary_injunction_application: A plaintiff sought an interim order restraining conduct while a civil suit was pending.
predicates.prima_facie_case: The court found that the plaintiff had an arguable case concerning breach of an agreement.
predicates.alternative_damages_claimed: The plaintiff pleaded damages as an alternative remedy and stated monetary estimates for losses alleged to result from the breach.
predicates.financial_injury_compensable_by_damages: The injury relied on was financial and the court found that damages could adequately compensate it.

issues.definition: When a plaintiff seeking a temporary injunction has a prima facie case but claims financial losses that damages can adequately compensate, the injunction is denied.

issues.legal_issue: Temporary injunctions are governed by the Code of Civil Procedure rather than the substantive provisions of the Specific Relief Act.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought a temporary injunction under Order 39 Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, read with Section 151, while seeking specific performance in the underlying suit.
The parties raised arguments based on Sections 14, 41, and 42 of the Specific Relief Act concerning specific performance and injunctions.
issues.conclusion: The court did not need to decide the parties’ arguments under Sections 14, 41, and 42 because temporary injunctions are regulated by the Code of Civil Procedure.
issues.legal_principle: Section 37 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 provides that temporary injunctions are regulated by the Code of Civil Procedure. The court applied that provision to the application made under Order 39 Rules 1 and 2 of the Code.

predicates.temporary_injunction_pending_civil_suit: A party sought an interim injunction while a civil suit was pending.

issues.definition: When an interim injunction is sought during a pending civil suit, its regulation is governed by civil procedure.
